title: Program Execution and Performance Tuning in GPUs
learningGoals: Explain why performance tuning matters: two programs doing the same task can perform very differently.
Describe the GPU memory hierarchy (registers → shared/L1 → L2 → global/VRAM → host RAM), with access cycles, scope and sizes.
Convert cycles into time (for example, 1 cycle at 1.5 GHz ≈ 0.67 ns).
Explain naive vs tiled matrix multiplication using shared memory and locality.
Explain how neural-network operations (element-wise, reduction, dot product) map onto GPU threads.
Know the basic performance metrics: kernel time, memory bandwidth, occupancy, efficiency.
sirStressed: "Tuning to the underlying GPU is very, very important." Small savings × millions of operations = big gains.
Memory hierarchy with cycle counts: registers 1, shared/L1 5, L2 50–100, global 400–800, host thousands. Closer = faster, but smaller.
One cycle = one tick of the GPU clock. At 1.5 GHz that's ≈ 0.67 ns. Be ready to calculate this.
Host → device is the costliest move. Move large chunks in one shot. "Minimise the data movement."
Matrix multiplication is the canonical example: locality-aware programs, tiling and shared memory give a multi-fold speed-up.
NNs = layers of maths, mostly multiplication and addition (element-wise, reduction, dot product), which is why GPUs enable real-time AI.
commonTraps: Order of the pyramid: registers (top, fastest) → shared/L1 → L2 → global → host (bottom, slowest).
Scope: registers = per thread; shared memory = per block; L2 = chip-wide; global = all threads of the GPU.
Thinking tiling reduces the number of multiplications. It doesn't. It reduces global memory reads through reuse.
Mixing up a reduction (many → one) with element-wise (one → one for each element).
Counting only kernel time. Total time includes the PCIe transfers.
summary: Tuning matters: core occupancy, choice of memory, number of transfers.

Pyramid: registers (per thread, KB, 1 cycle) → shared/L1 (per block, ~5) → constant/texture (read-only) → L2 (chip-wide, ~50 MB, 50–100) → global VRAM (off-chip, 400–800) → host RAM (thousands, via PCIe/NVLink).
1 cycle at 1.5 GHz ≈ 0.67 ns. Data-hungry cores sit idle if data is late.
Rules: move big chunks once; reuse data; compute more, move less.

Matmul: naive = repeated global reads. Tiled = load tiles (for example 16×16 of 1024×1024) into shared memory, reuse them across the block's threads, one block per output tile, sync, then a multi-fold (10×+) speed-up.

NN: neuron = weighted sum + bias + activation. Operations: element-wise (bias/activation, one thread per element; the JEE grace-marks analogy), reduction (sum → one value), dot product (multiply pairs and add). GPUs do layers in ms, enabling real-time AI (live translation, self-driving).
Metrics: kernel time, bandwidth, occupancy, efficiency, speed-up. Profilers: Nsight, PyTorch profiler.

questions.prompt: Why are GPUs important for AI and data science?

options.text: They allow parallel execution of many data operations

questions.prompt: Which best describes the GPU's role in modern computing?

options.text: It accelerates highly parallel tasks such as graphics and ML

questions.prompt: GPU vs CPU: which is true?

options.text: GPUs contain thousands of smaller, efficient cores

questions.explanation: many simple cores vs a few powerful ones.

questions.prompt: What does "data movement cost" mean?

options.text: The time and energy needed to move data between memory levels

questions.explanation: for example, a global access takes 400–800 cycles vs ~5 for shared memory.

questions.prompt: Why is understanding the memory hierarchy essential?

options.text: To optimise data movement and reduce latency

questions.prompt: Which GPU memory is shared, fastest, but small?
questions.explanation: registers are faster but private to each thread. Among the memories threads can share, on-chip shared memory is the fastest.

questions.prompt: What is tiling?

options.text: Dividing data into smaller blocks to make better use of the cache/shared memory

questions.explanation: tiles are loaded into shared memory once and reused by the whole block.

questions.prompt: Why is matrix multiplication ideal for GPUs?

options.text: Each element can be computed independently

questions.explanation: each C[i][j] is its own dot product, so it can be one thread each.

questions.prompt: How does multi-threading speed up matrix multiplication?
questions.explanation: the amount of work stays the same; it just happens in parallel.

questions.prompt: What are element-wise operations?

options.text: One whole data set at once
Applying a computation to each element individually

questions.explanation: for example, adding a bias or applying ReLU, with one thread per element. Option C describes a reduction.

questions.prompt: Dot-product operations on GPUs are:

options.text: Basic building blocks of neural-network layers

questions.explanation: each neuron computes a weighted sum, which is a dot product.

questions.prompt: Why do NN operations perform well on GPUs?
Why analyse kernel performance before optimising?

options.text: To identify memory bottlenecks and compute imbalance

questions.explanation: measure first, then optimise (the same rule as profiling in Week 8).

questions.prompt: What is occupancy?

options.text: The percentage of GPU cores (warp slots) actively executing threads

questions.prompt: Which factor affects GPU performance the most?

options.text: Thread count and memory access patterns

questions.explanation: occupancy plus coalesced memory access.

questions.prompt: GPUs differ from CPUs mainly because they:

options.text: Use slower cores for sequential logic

questions.prompt: Why should programmers understand GPU memory?

options.text: To optimise data placement for faster access

questions.prompt: What is the ultimate goal of GPU performance tuning?
Which GPU memory is fastest and private to each thread?
questions.explanation: Registers: per thread, 1 cycle.

questions.prompt: Shared memory is shared by:
questions.explanation: All threads of a block.

questions.prompt: Which data movement is generally the most expensive?
questions.explanation: Host → device over PCIe/NVLink takes thousands of cycles.

questions.prompt: Tiling in matrix multiplication mainly reduces:
questions.explanation: Tiling reuses tiles held in shared memory. The FLOP count stays the same.

questions.prompt: Adding the same bias to every element of a vector is a(n):
questions.explanation: Element-wise (one thread per element).

questions.prompt: Which memory is read-only and specialised for constants or graphics access patterns?
questions.explanation: Constant/texture memory.

questions.prompt: A GPU runs at 2 GHz. How long is one cycle? Estimate the time for one shared-memory access (5 cycles) and one global access (600 cycles).
Compute the dot product of [2, 0, 3, 1] and [1, 4, 2, 5], and explain how a GPU would parallelise it.
correctAnswers: 2·1 + 0·4 + 3·2 + 1·5 = 2 + 0 + 6 + 5 = 13. The GPU uses 4 threads to multiply the pairs in parallel, then a parallel reduction (2 + 0 = 2 and 6 + 5 = 11, then 2 + 11 = 13) in log₂4 = 2 steps.
questions.explanation: 2·1 + 0·4 + 3·2 + 1·5 = 2 + 0 + 6 + 5 = 13. The GPU uses 4 threads to multiply the pairs in parallel, then a parallel reduction (2 + 0 = 2 and 6 + 5 = 11, then 2 + 11 = 13) in log₂4 = 2 steps.

questions.prompt: A student's matrix-multiplication kernel for a 2048×2048 matrix reads every A and B element directly from global memory, and the GPU sits mostly idle. Diagnose the problem and describe the fix.
correctAnswers: The kernel is memory-bound. It makes repeated global memory reads at 400–800 cycles each, so the cores starve. Fix: a tiled kernel. Load 16×16 (or 32×32) tiles of A and B into shared memory, sync, let every thread in the block reuse the tiles, have each block compute one output tile of C, and loop over the tile pairs. Also keep the matrices on the GPU and use coalesced loads.
questions.explanation: The kernel is memory-bound. It makes repeated global memory reads at 400–800 cycles each, so the cores starve. Fix: a tiled kernel. Load 16×16 (or 32×32) tiles of A and B into shared memory, sync, let every thread in the block reuse the tiles, have each block compute one output tile of C, and loop over the tile pairs. Also keep the matrices on the GPU and use coalesced loads.

questions.prompt: List the memory levels from fastest to slowest, with approximate access cycles.
correctAnswers: Registers (1) → shared/L1/constant cache (~5) → L2 (50–100) → global VRAM (400–800) → host RAM (thousands).
